lesson.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specAnchors.text: understand that bile is produced by the liver and stored in the gall bladder
understand the role of bile in neutralising stomach acid and emulsifying lipids

primer.text: You have met the stomach's acid and the intestine's enzymes in passing. This short lesson slots bile between them: where the liver makes it, where the gall bladder parks it, and the two jobs — neutralising acid and emulsifying fat — that let the small intestine's enzymes work at their best.

modules.title: Bile: Made by the Liver, Working in the Gut
modules.opening: Bile is an alkaline fluid — the liver makes it, the gall bladder stores it — until the small intestine needs it. There it does two jobs at once: it neutralises the acidic chyme arriving from the stomach, and its salts emulsify large fat drops into many tiny ones, multiplying the surface that lipase can attack.
keyPoints: Cells in the liver produce bile, an alkaline substance.
The gall bladder stores bile before release into the small intestine.
Bile neutralises hydrochloric acid arriving from the stomach.
Intestinal enzymes work best at a higher, more alkaline optimum pH.
Emulsification breaks large lipid drops into smaller ones with more surface area.
With alkaline conditions and extra surface, lipase converts lipid to glycerol and fatty acids faster.

low.restatement: Liver makes it, gall bladder stores it, gut benefits twice.
low.analogy: A delivery van: stocked at the depot (gall bladder), unloading where the work is (intestine).
low.examPointer: Name both organs of production and storage — each carries a mark.

medium.restatement: Bile's two roles are physical and chemical setup: neutralise the pH, then multiply the surface for enzymes.
medium.analogy: Preparing a workshop: clean the bench (neutralise), then spread out the parts (emulsify).
medium.examPointer: Remember emulsification is mechanical digestion — no bonds are broken.

glossary.definition: The alkaline fluid made by the liver, stored in the gall bladder, that neutralises acid and emulsifies fat.
Breaking large lipid drops into many smaller ones, mechanical digestion that raises surface area.
The acidity at which an enzyme works fastest; intestinal enzymes prefer alkaline conditions.
